rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4, 6.1-6.6, Tables 1-7 and Fig. 11 report the author's own prototype (Arduino, HL-69 soil hygrometer, DHT22, BH1750 light, SEN0169 pH sensors, GSM module), a training dataset, and KNN model runs with precision/recall/F1 and error-rate-versus-k results.
rows.notes: The study contains no EC sensor and no salinity measurement or result; the only soil chemistry sensor is pH (Section 4.1.4), used to trigger a fertiliser notification (Section 6.4), not to mitigate salinity. No soil-health outcome is reported. The study's own results are limited to KNN classification accuracy (98.6%, RMSE 0.1, Tables 5-7) and a deployed prototype with no measured field effect on salinity or over-irrigation.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4 and 6, Tables 1-7, Fig. 11 report the author's own IoT prototype with soil moisture and weather forecast inputs and KNN model runs with accuracy, error rate, precision/recall/F1.
rows.notes: The study does test an IoT/app scheduling system using soil moisture and weather forecast data (though without EC), but it reports no measurement of irrigation water applied, water saved or over-irrigation avoided. The abstract and conclusion assert that the prototype leads to efficient and economical water use and reduced water use, but the only quantified results are KNN classification accuracy (98.6%, RMSE 0.1) and mean error versus k (Table 5, Fig. 11); the 20% rain-saving example is a design rule, not a measured outcome. Classification of irrigation need is at most a precondition for preventing over-irrigation, so upstream is set true. EC component absent, noted as partial mismatch but technology category (app scheduling) matches.

notes: Full text appears complete.
